youtube_title: They Copied a Rival's Phone Book — and Won at the Supreme Court 🦝⚖️
caption: Feist v. Rural (1991): copying phone listings wasn't copyright infringement, because facts aren't copyrightable and an alphabetical list isn't original. 'Copyright rewards originality, not effort.'
script: They copied a competitor's phone listings, and won at the Supreme Court. This is Feist versus Rural Telephone, from nineteen ninety-one. Rural Telephone, a utility in Kansas, published a phone book. Feist made bigger regional directories and asked to license Rural's white-pages listings. Rural said no. So Feist copied them anyway, one thousand three hundred nine listings. And four of those were fake listings Rural had planted to catch copiers. Caught red-handed, right? Rural sued for copyright infringement and won in the lower courts. But the Supreme Court reversed. Names, towns and phone numbers are facts. And copyright, the Court said, can never extend to the facts themselves. A collection of facts is protected only for original choices in selecting or arranging them, and the Court said there's nothing remotely creative about listing names alphabetically. It also rejected the idea that hard work alone earns a copyright. In its words, copyright rewards originality, not effort. Here's the limit. Original writing, and creative choices about what to include and how to arrange it, can still be protected. Rural's phone book as a whole still had a copyright. And this isn't permission to copy whole websites. Privacy laws, contracts and site terms are separate issues. [loop] So before you copy someone's phone book, remember
